content: Palliative care in residential care facilities for older individuals can significantly reduce hospital referrals. This approach not only improves the quality of life for patients but also decreases overall healthcare costs by minimizing avoidable hospitalizations, emergency department visits, and unnecessary treatments. The cost of palliative care includes both direct and indirect expenses. Direct costs are further divided into fixed and variable expenses. It is essential to establish a measurement framework for planning purposes, which could include metrics such as total annual budget, cost per day, cost per patient per month, cost per inpatient day, cost per inpatient episode of care, or cost per home or clinic visit. Unlike other healthcare services, the primary cost driver in palliative care is personnel expenses, as opposed to the higher treatment costs seen in other medical services. Funding remains a critical issue, as most palliative care services must adapt to the financial resources available to them. A costing model from Romania calculates four key metrics: cost per inpatient day, cost per home visit, home-care cost per month, and cost per case. This model uses local costs for personnel, medications, supplies, and other items to generate results. For example, the average cost per episode of home care, which includes approximately 45 visits, is calculated. In South Africa, the average monthly cost for home care is $96, while the cost per inpatient day is $91. However, palliative care costs are only one part of the equation. These expenses can be offset by reductions in other areas, particularly hospitalizations. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides guidelines and essential medicine lists for palliative care, including non-opioid and opioid analgesics, as well as medications for managing other common symptoms. For example, morphine is available in various forms, such as granules, injections, oral liquids, and slow-release tablets. Other medications include amitriptyline, cyclizine, dexamethasone, and ondansetron, among others, tailored to address specific symptoms in palliative care settings. The WHO also emphasizes the importance of planning and implementing palliative care services, providing resources for program managers to develop effective and sustainable care models.
